title: Report across tables
one: A report that joins tables, filters by dates and shows totals.
marks: This chapter is where the examiner looks for a query that reaches across several tables to answer a real question, and for a mistake that is caught with a sentence instead of a crash.

blocks.p: Every screen so far has shown one table and changed it. A report is different. A report asks one question of the whole database, for a range of dates, and shows the answer in a grid. Which mechanic did the most work in March? Where did the money come from last week? Which service is booked most? Each question needs rows from two, three or four tables at once.

words: Report
A question asked of the whole database for a range of dates, answered as a grid of rows.
Date range
Two dates, From and To, with every day between them counted in.
LEFT JOIN
A join that keeps every row of the first table, even the rows that match nothing in the second.
GROUP BY
The words that squash many rows into one row per thing, so COUNT and SUM can add them up.
UNION ALL
The words that stack the rows of one SELECT under the rows of another, as one list.
Derived table
A SELECT inside brackets that another SELECT reads from, as if it were a table.
ISNULL
A function that swaps an empty value for the value you give it, such as 0.
DATEDIFF
A function that counts the minutes, hours or days between two times.
Exception
An object that a method throws when something has gone wrong, carrying a sentence that says what.
Catch
The part of a method that takes an exception and does something sensible with it, instead of crashing.

screens.title: Read what a report does, and what it never does.

blocks.p: A report is three things: one question, two dates, one grid. The question is fixed in the stored procedure. The dates come from the form. The grid is whatever rows the SELECT makes. Nothing else is needed, because the answer is read straight from the tables that your screens have been keeping right since chapter 6.

box.title: The five questions Towpath Cycles asks
box.text: Which mechanic did the most work, and earned the most for the shop? Where did the money come from, day by day, and was it the workshop, bike hire or parts? How much happened: how many bookings, hires, sales and orders? Which services are booked most? Which parts sell most? Each question is one stored procedure, and each stored procedure is one SELECT, or a stack of SELECTs.

blocks.p: A report never changes data. There is no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in any of the five. That is why none of them has an @Message parameter: there is nothing to refuse. In the program, each one is called with Db.GetTable, which hands back a table of rows, never with Db.Run. Run the same report twice and you get the same answer twice, and the database is exactly as it was.

stages.title: Which mechanic did the most work

screens.title: Read the workload stored procedure, then add it to your script.

blocks.p: The first report answers one question: for each mechanic, how many jobs were done between two dates, how many hours did they take, and how much did the shop earn from them. Three tables take part. Staff gives the mechanics, Appointment gives the jobs, and ServiceType gives the price of each job. Read the stored procedure below first. It uses a LEFT JOIN so a mechanic with no jobs still shows, a GROUP BY so there is one row per mechanic, and COUNT, SUM and DATEDIFF to count the jobs and add up the minutes and the money.

code.title: usp_Report_MechanicWorkload: jobs, hours and income per mechanic
parts: The name, and the two dates that go in
Every report takes the same two things: a From date and a To date. Nothing comes back through a parameter. The answer is the table of rows that the SELECT makes.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.
The first name, a space and the last name are joined into one piece of text with plus signs. AS Mechanic names the column, so the grid heading reads Mechanic and not an expression.
The second column: how many jobs
COUNT counts the appointment numbers in the group. It counts the appointment column, not a star, because a mechanic with no jobs has no appointment number and must count as 0, not 1.

DATEDIFF counts the minutes from the start of each job to its end. SUM adds the minutes up. ISNULL turns an empty total into 0 for a mechanic with no jobs. Dividing by 60.0 makes hours, and CAST to DECIMAL(6,1) rounds the answer to one decimal place, such as 2.8.
The price of each job comes from its service type. SUM adds the prices up, and ISNULL gives 0 to a mechanic with nothing to add.
Start from the staff, and bring in their jobs

The report starts from Staff, because the question is about mechanics. LEFT JOIN brings in each mechanic's appointments, and keeps the mechanic even when none match. The three tests after ON pick which appointments count: the mechanic's own, finished ones, and ones that started between the two dates. CAST to DATE throws away the clock part so that BETWEEN works on whole days. The date test sits after ON and not in a WHERE on purpose: a WHERE would throw away the mechanics with no jobs in those dates.
Bring in the price of each job
Each appointment has a service type, and the service type holds the price. This is a LEFT JOIN too, so a mechanic with no appointments, and so no service type, is still kept.
Staff holds the manager and the counter staff too. The WHERE is on the Staff row, so it keeps the right people without losing anyone's jobs.
GROUP BY squashes all of one mechanic's appointment rows into one row, so that COUNT and SUM have something to add up. Every column in the SELECT that is not inside COUNT or SUM must be listed here.
DESC means highest first. Two mechanics with the same income are then put in name order, so the list is always in the same order. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Report_MechanicWorkload
    @FromDate DATE,
    @ToDate   DATE
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT s.FirstName + ' ' + s.LastName AS Mechanic,
           COUNT(a.AppointmentID) AS JobsDone,
           CAST(ISNULL(SUM(DATEDIFF(MINUTE, a.StartTime, a.EndTime)), 0) / 60.0
               AS DECIMAL(6,1)) AS HoursWorked,
           ISNULL(SUM(st.Price), 0) AS Income
    FROM Staff s
    LEFT JOIN Appointment a
           ON a.MechanicID = s.StaffID
          AND a.Status = 'Done'
          AND CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate
    LEFT JOIN ServiceType st ON st.ServiceTypeID = a.ServiceTypeID
    WHERE s.Role = 'Mechanic'
    GROUP BY s.StaffID, s.FirstName, s.LastName
    ORDER BY Income DESC, Mechanic;
END
GO

screens.title: Read the income stored procedure, and type the lines that stack it.

blocks.p: Money comes into the shop from three places: the workshop, bike hire and parts. They live in three different tables. The second report puts all three into one grid, one row per day per source, by stacking three SELECTs on top of each other with UNION ALL. The three SELECTs must have the same columns in the same order. The whole stack sits inside brackets as a derived table, so that one ORDER BY at the end can sort every row by day. You type the seams, where one part ends and the next begins, so that you see the columns lining up with your own hands. Add it in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) the same way as before.

code.title: usp_Report_Income: the money per day, from three tables
parts: The name, and the two dates that go in
Every report takes the same two things: a From date and a To date. Nothing comes back through a parameter. The answer is the table of rows that the SELECT makes.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.
The outer SELECT: four columns from a stack
This SELECT reads from the bracket that follows, not from a table. Day is in square brackets because SQL Server uses that word itself. The four names are the column headings the grid will show.

One row per day of finished jobs: the day, the word Workshop as its source, how many jobs, and the prices added up. Appointment is joined to ServiceType for the price. The AS names here name the columns for the whole stack, because the first SELECT names the columns for all of them.
The first seam: the yellow lines

GROUP BY on the day ends the workshop part. UNION ALL stacks the next part underneath. The SELECT that starts the bike hire part gives the same four things: a day, the words Bike hire in quotes, a count and a sum. It has no AS names, because the first part named the columns already.
Where the hire money comes from
Only hires that came back count, on the day they came back. EndDate is already a date, so no CAST is needed.
The second seam: the yellow lines

The same shape again. GROUP BY on the day ends the hire part, UNION ALL stacks the parts sales underneath, and the SELECT gives a day, the word Parts, and a count. The count here is a SUM of quantities, because one sale can be three inner tubes.
Where the parts money comes from
The income of a sale is its quantity times the price it was sold at. Only sales still marked Sold count, so a refund drops out. CAST to DATE throws away the clock part of SoldOn.
Close the stack and sort it

The closing bracket ends the derived table, and AS income gives it a name, which SQL Server insists on. ORDER BY sorts the whole stack by day, then by source, so the three sources of one day sit together. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.why: Each yellow block is a seam: the GROUP BY that ends one part, UNION ALL, and the SELECT that starts the next. The SELECT you type must give the same four columns, in the same order, as the workshop part above it. Typing it is how you learn to line them up.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Report_Income
    @FromDate DATE,
    @ToDate   DATE
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT [Day], Source, Items, Income
    FROM (
        SELECT CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE) AS [Day], 'Workshop' AS Source,
               COUNT(*) AS Items, SUM(st.Price) AS Income
        FROM Appointment a
        JOIN ServiceType st ON st.ServiceTypeID = a.ServiceTypeID
        WHERE a.Status = 'Done' AND CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate
            AND @ToDate
        GROUP BY CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE)

        UNION ALL

        SELECT h.EndDate, 'Bike hire', COUNT(*), SUM(h.TotalCost)
        FROM Hire h
        WHERE h.Status = 'Returned' AND h.EndDate BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate
        GROUP BY h.EndDate

        UNION ALL

        SELECT CAST(ps.SoldOn AS DATE), 'Parts', SUM(ps.Quantity),
            SUM(ps.Quantity * ps.UnitPrice)
        FROM PartSale ps
        WHERE ps.Status = 'Sold' AND CAST(ps.SoldOn AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate
            AND @ToDate
        GROUP BY CAST(ps.SoldOn AS DATE)
    ) AS income
    ORDER BY [Day], Source;
END
GO

screens.title: Type the four stacked counts of the activity stored procedure.

blocks.p: The third report is five numbers: bookings kept, bookings cancelled, hires, parts sold and orders placed, each between the two dates. Each number is one small SELECT that gives one row with a label and a count, and UNION ALL stacks the five rows into one grid. The label is text in quotes, so the first column reads Workshop bookings and not a column name. The first SELECT is given. In SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), you type the other four from its pattern: same shape, a different table, a different status test.

code.title: usp_Report_Activity: five counts in one grid
parts: The name, and the two dates that go in
Every report takes the same two things: a From date and a To date. Nothing comes back through a parameter. The answer is the table of rows that the SELECT makes.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.
AND CAST(StartTime AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate

The text in quotes is the label, and AS [What] names the column. COUNT(*) counts the appointment rows that are not cancelled and started between the dates. How many is in square brackets because it has a space in it. This SELECT names the two columns for the whole stack.
AND CAST(StartTime AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate
UNION ALL stacks one more row underneath. The same table, with the status test turned round: only the cancelled ones. No AS names, because the first SELECT named the columns.
Hires that were not cancelled and started between the dates. StartDate is already a date, so there is no CAST.
AND CAST(SoldOn AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate
This one is a SUM, not a COUNT, because one sale row can be three inner tubes. ISNULL turns an empty sum into 0 when nothing was sold, so the row still appears with a number in it.

Orders that were not cancelled and were placed between the dates. The last line ends with a semicolon, because it is the end of the whole stacked statement. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.

CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Report_Activity
    @FromDate DATE,
    @ToDate   DATE
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT 'Workshop bookings' AS [What], COUNT(*) AS [How many]
    FROM Appointment

blocks.p: The fourth report lists every service with how many times it was booked between the dates, most booked first. It lists every service, including the ones nobody booked: a manager wants to see the 0 beside Safety check, not wonder where it went. That is a LEFT JOIN from ServiceType to Appointment, with the date test after ON, the same shape as the workload report. Read the stored procedure below, then add it to your script in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). The next screen breaks the report on purpose, so that you see what the LEFT does.

code.title: usp_Report_PopularServices: every service, most booked first
parts: The name, and the two dates that go in
Every report takes the same two things: a From date and a To date. Nothing comes back through a parameter. The answer is the table of rows that the SELECT makes.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.
The service's name, how many appointments matched it, and its price. COUNT on the appointment number gives 0 for a service with no matching appointments, because there are no numbers to count.
The report starts from ServiceType, because the question is about services. Every row of this table will be in the answer.

LEFT JOIN keeps every service even when no appointment matches. The three tests after ON pick the appointments that count: the right service, not cancelled, and started between the dates. The date test must sit here, after ON. If it moved to a WHERE, a service with no bookings in those dates would be thrown away, and the 0 would vanish with it.

code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Report_PopularServices
    @FromDate DATE,
    @ToDate   DATE
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT st.Name AS Service,
           COUNT(a.AppointmentID) AS Bookings,
           st.Price
    FROM ServiceType st
    LEFT JOIN Appointment a
           ON a.ServiceTypeID = st.ServiceTypeID
          AND a.Status <> 'Cancelled'
          AND CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE) BETWEEN @FromDate AND @ToDate
    GROUP BY st.ServiceTypeID, st.Name, st.Price
    ORDER BY Bookings DESC, Service;
END
GO

blocks.p: A report can be asked one impossible thing: a From date after the To date. The form could check the two boxes itself, but the check belongs with the data code, because every report needs it and the form should not have to remember. So the data class throws an exception. An exception is an object that a method throws when it cannot carry on, carrying a sentence that says why. The method that threw it stops at once, and the sentence travels up to whoever called it, until a catch takes it. The one class you write from nothing in Visual Studio 2019 is that exception.

The first line of the class ends with a colon and the word Exception. The colon means is a kind of: InvalidDateRangeException is a kind of Exception, and gets everything an Exception already has, such as its Message. The constructor passes its sentence to base, which is the Exception underneath, so the sentence becomes the Message. The form in the next stage catches this class by its name, so nothing else is caught by mistake.

blocks.p: Twelve ticks show that every report answers its question. They also show that a From date after the To date gives a sentence, and that two dates with nothing sold or booked between them give an empty grid and a sentence. They show that a service or a part nobody bought still appears in its report, and that taking LEFT out of the join loses the service. Last, they show that Copy to clipboard works and that counter staff cannot open the reports. When you want the sample data back, click in BikeShop.sql and press F5 with nothing selected.
